positive: Conversational/spoken-register discourse tokens in quoted speech or interviews: dashes and em-dashes that break off a thought, filler/hedge words like 'like', 'know' (as in 'you know'/'look like you know'), and hyphen pieces in compounds; informal quoted remarks from musicians/people in Wikipedia articles. Weak activations overall.
negative: Second token of a multi-token proper name or title, especially pop-culture names (e.g. 'Green [Lantern]' film title), and noun completions of character/role words like 'vigil[ante]', 'unlikely [hero]' -- names of heroes/franchises/film titles in release/sales contexts.

positive: Prepositions/function words that complete a fixed valence pattern of a preceding adjective, verb, or participle: 'sent [to]', 'new [to]', 'older [than]', 'best [of]', 'found [by]'. The preposition is grammatically required by the head word (comparatives -> 'than', passive participle -> 'by', 'to the best of'). Occurs in both prose and math reasoning.
negative: Articles/pronouns/prepositions inside song or film titles and idioms ('With [a] Little Help', 'To Catch [a] Thief'), object pronoun after 'took [it]', and 'with' introducing an accompaniment or circumstance ('returned with the emperor', 'but with the outbreak of') -- i.e. prepositions/determiners not governed by a preceding adjective/comparative.

positive: The list-item number at the start of a new line in markdown step-by-step math solutions, right after a blank line following a calculation ('\n\n3.  **'), and the space/number after 'Step' in '**Step 1:**'. I.e. tokens beginning a new numbered step section.
negative: The '$' opening an inline math expression right after a colon label in a bullet list ('Milk: $5 \times', 'Small boxes: $9'), and '=' in display equations; i.e. the start of a calculation within a bullet item. Also rare unrelated name subwords.

positive: Start of a year or number in a date or sequence where a continuation is predictable: the first digit of a year following 'day Month' ('1 January [1]900', '28 February [2]000'), the next item in an enumerated series of ordinals ('8th, 9th, [ ]10th'), 'and' joining consecutive months ('September [and] October'), and the first digit of a dollar amount after '$'. Fires strongly on dates/calendar sequences.
negative: Mid-word subword tokens of rare proper names and words (e.g. 'Gipsy [Mo]th', 'he [mo]ans', 'Mil[ha]ud'), and number after 'Every' in a periodic interval ('Every [ ]7 days'), 'squares of [perfect]'.

positive: Tokens inside proper names of institutions, products, and technical/military specifications in encyclopedic text: words in organization/act names ('Indian [Arts] and Crafts Act', 'Elswick [Ordn]ance Company'), platform names ('GameCube and [Windows]'), year digits in naval history ('1[9]06'), units like 'long tons'. Mostly naval/military/technical Wikipedia.
negative: Content words inside government/organization names of ministries and agencies ('Minister of [Foreign] Affairs', 'Food and [Agriculture] Organization'), economic words like 'regional [trade]', and subword pieces of food words ('cuc[um]bers', 'Savory [Sou]fflés').

positive: Mixed: word predicting a comparison/relation complement ('is [closest] to', 'found to [be] closely related'), LaTeX operator backslash in math expressions ('\right) [\]div'), mid-word pieces of names and digits within numbers ('10[0]1'). Weak, diffuse.
negative: First subword of romanized Chinese or other non-English proper names/places ('Nanjing [Gu]ozijian', '[Hu]', '[Gu]adeloupe', '[Su]ai'), especially Chinese surnames/place syllables like Gu, Hu, Su; also 'what is [the] maximum' in math question stems.

positive: Variable-definition setup in structured math reasoning: the "'s" in "let's call it/this $x$", the '*' bullet starting a new 'Let $X$ represent...' line, and ':**' closing a bold heading like '**Identify the Variables:**'. Fires when the model is about to introduce/define a variable symbol.
negative: Conversational or reflective prose transitions: opening quote mark of reported speech after 'said ,', sentence-initial 'Here is', 'Looks [good]' verification remarks after a computation, and commas in literary/poetic first-person text.

positive: LaTeX tokens in math expressions inside $...$ immediately after a number or operator, specifically backslash commands starting '\text{' or '\times' and '(\' opening '(\text{...})' -- e.g. '40 [\]text{ classes}', '$24 - [(\]text{', '20,000 [\]times'. Very strong on units/labels written with \text after a number.
negative: Mid-name tokens in sports and military/historical Wikipedia text: 'FIBA [U]19', 'Division [I]', 'the [Canadian] Player of', 'North[c]ote', 'Sugar [Lo]af'; capitalized name/title pieces within proper nouns.

positive: Subword continuation tokens completing rare or foreign words and surnames, especially after a name start: 'Kör[ting]', 'cor[set]', 'C[odd]', 'Self-C[or]rection', 'Bullec[ourt]' (German/French names and places). Fires on the second/later piece of a word split into pieces.
negative: The word 'well' in the fixed phrase 'as [well] as', and endings of common words split in pieces ('camar[ader]ie', 'cou[gars]').

positive: The particle/preposition 'off' after motion or removal verbs: 'kick things [off]', 'jumped [off]', 'thrown X [off] the stage', 'pushing X [off]', 'pulled one person [off]'. Phrasal verbs of displacement, especially 'off' (the stage).
negative: Completion adverbs/adjectives after a verb denoting manner or totality: 'dissipate [entirely]', 'Dreams Come [True]', 'driving [straight]', 'cease [all]' -- words completing verb phrases that are not 'off'.
